items.title: 7 Best PS5 JRPGs That You Need to Play in Fall 2026
items.summary: Some JRPGs are perfect for fall, and these ones on the PS5 are the perfect games to play this fall.
items.content:
By Shayna Josi Published Oct 19, 2026, 10:30 AM EDT Shayna Josi is a Contributor at DualShockers who covers RPGs, cozy games, life sims, action games, gamer culture, and PC gaming. She has been writing professionally since 2020 and covering games since 2023, with a focus on features, commentary, storytelling, character writing, and game design.

Fall brings cooler weather and shorter days, something that depresses many but also makes for perfect gaming weather. The PS5 has produced some great JRPGs , and fall is one of the best times to catch up on your gaming backlog and get around to the games that you know you'll enjoy but just can't get around to.

Here are the most addictive JRPGs that you can play on the PlayStation 5 right now.

These PS5 JRPGs range from bright and sunny to transport you to sunnier destinations on gloomy days. It also includes classic games that every JRPG fan should play, or that align neatly with the fall themes of change and endings. No matter your taste, there's something here for everyone.

Expand Collapse Final Fantasy Resonance releases in late October. It's actually an adaptation of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, a free-to-play mobile game that's been shut down since 2024. The adaptation to PS5 and other modern consoles is an exciting prospect, and it brings some classic FF mechanics that haven't been used in a while, like turn-based combat.

FF Resonance will likely become a good place to start if you haven't played any other FF. Getting into the Final Fantasy franchise can be confusing because there are so many games, with some of them being inaccessible because of how old they are, sequels, or just bad starting points. As Resonance is based on a standalone game, it may be the perfect place to dive into FF this fall.

Metaphor: ReFantazio RPG JRPG Action Adventure 9 /10

Expand Collapse Metaphor: ReFantazio took the gaming world by storm when it was released in 2024. It took home Best RPG of the Year at the Game Awards, and has been praised for its incredible art, story, and characters. It also has a great turn-based combat system, and is a great place to start if you either have never played turn-based combat or have historically disliked it.

Metaphor: ReFantazio's sprawling setting and storyline are perfect to explore thanks to the crisp days and long nights of fall. It's a project in itself to complete, even more so to Platinum, so it's a great choice if you're looking for just one game to soak up your time before the winter holidays.

Expand Collapse The Persona series is one of the most well-known and popular of JRPGs, and has gone on to influence many of the most successful video game developers. Persona 3 Reload is a 2024 remake of the original Persona 3, which had an original release in 2006.

Time erases everything, but it shouldn't erase these JRPGs from our memories.

Persona 3 Reload's school setting is perfect for back-to-school vibes that encapsulate fall. It also has a story darker than some of the other entries on this list, and that moody vibe matches well with moody weather, longer nights, and falling leaves. Persona 3 Reload's more quiet, introspective approach to character growth is also deeply appropriate for long nights spent indoors.

Expand Collapse In contrast to some of the other games on this list, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth has the exact opposite weather and vibe to fall, and takes place in a tropical paradise. Sometimes, though, a change of scenery is exactly what you need when SAD hits.

Infinite Wealth's scope is massive, and a single playthrough can often take more than 100 hours . It offers a lot here, and working through it all will likely take up the entirety of your fall. There's also some surprisingly cozy gameplay with Dondoko Island, which involves customizing a tropical island. If you can't actually escape the cold to a tropical island, Infinite Wealth is the closest second.

items.title: You Can Play Battlefield 6 and More on Xbox Game Pass Now
items.summary: However, Clair Obscur is now gone from the service. Je suis désolé.
items.content:
However, Clair Obscur is now gone from the service. Je suis désolé.

Microsoft Xbox Game Pass subscribers can now jump into huge battles in Battlefield 6. That’s welcome news, because Microsoft removed one of CNET’s best games of 2025, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , from the service. Maybe Battlefield 6 and the other games that arrived on the service this month will have what it takes to fill the Clair Obscur-sized hole in my heart.

Xbox Game Pass , a CNET Editors’ Choice award pick, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X , Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 a month . With a subscription to the higher-tiered Game Pass Ultimate ( $23 a month ), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones the day they’re released, each month.

Here are all the games Microsoft added to Xbox Game Pass in the first half of October 2026.

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

CNET’s David Lumb called this installment in the popular Battlefield series a “ riveting shooter .” It’s full of huge multiplayer battles, close-quarters combat and loads of gunfights and explosions. While most people will gravitate toward multiplayer, there is a single-player campaign if you want a break from the online mayhem.

In this first-person soulslike game, you’re a soldier in Napoleon’s army who dies. Not to worry, because you’re back from the dead with a handful of supernatural abilities that you wield in your left hand, like in the almost 20-year-old game BioShock . You’ll use these skills to battle monsters and uncover a conspiracy that could threaten all of humanity.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps proves that not every game coming to Game Pass has to be full of action. You’ll unwind and explore Bluey’s world while taking photos in areas familiar to anyone who’s seen the popular children’s show – let’s be honest, this show’s also popular with adults. You can take photos on your own or play with a partner, friend or your kid as you turn in-game moments into fun.

Those are a few of the games Microsoft brought to Game Pass in October. Here are the rest of the games you can see on the service now.

Microsoft also removed nine games from Xbox Game Pass, including the award-winning Clair Obscur. So you’ll have to buy these games separately now if you still want to play them.

For more on Xbox, check out our Xbox Game Pass review , learn which Game Pass plan is right for you and discover what other games you can play on the service.

items.title: GTA 6 squeaks into eligibility for The Game Awards 2026 by the smallest of margins - but can it break Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's record number of wins?
items.summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 releases 19th November and The Game Awards cut-off is 20th November. It's a close call. But will GTA 6 win?
items.content:
Image credit: Rockstar News by Robert Purchese Associate Editor Published on Oct. 15, 2026, 4:10 p.m. 48 comments Follow Grand Theft Auto VI Prioritise us on Google This generation's mega-game, Grand Theft Auto 6 , will be eligible for The Game Awards 2026 by a matter of one day.

As highlighted on X by industry watcher Shinobi602 , the cut-off date for this year's The Game Awards is 20th November, meaning GTA 6 - which arrives on 19th November - can be nominated across the show's various categories in 2026 and can potentially win. "Games must be made commercially available to customers on or before Friday, November 20, 2026, at 9pm PT," The Game Awards' website FAQ states.

The fit is so snug it might appear an exception has been made for Rockstar's game, but as Shinobi602 also noted , cut-off dates have been pretty similar each year, varying only by a day or two.

With GTA 6 in contention, the question becomes one of how much it could dominate proceedings. Rewind to Rockstar's last big release - Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018 - and that game took home four awards : Best Narrative, Best Audio Design, Best Score/Music, and Best Performance (won by Roger Clark for his portrayal of protagonist Arthur Morgan).

The current TGA record holder - the game to beat - is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , which last year took home nine wins , including the coveted Game of the Year award. Before Clair Obscur, the previous leader was Baldur's Gate 3 , with six wins. GTA 6 is an order of magnitude larger in terms of budget, scope, and public anticipation than either game, especially Clair Obscur. The weight of expectation is on Rockstar, that's for sure.

The Game Awards 2026 takes place on 10th December, and usually bookends the year's industry activity, after which we all frantically try to decide what our personal games of the year are. Eurogamer, for full disclosure, is a member of The Game Awards jury, along with many other gaming websites.

Meanwhile, Rockstar released a new launch trailer for GTA 6 this afternoon, highlighting Jason and Lucia's steamy relationship - literally, as they frolic in the shower - and the strain of being in a high-stakes crime environment such as theirs.

Rockstar is also currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland revolving around the sudden firing of 31 staff from Rockstar North last year. Those affected call it union-busting, whereas Rockstar insists employees were fired for gross misconduct. The verdict is now not expected until well into November , almost bang on when GTA 6 releases.

items.title: Game Pass Is About To Lose Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 And Some Other Incredible Games
items.summary: The RPG sensation and more gems are leaving in October
items.content:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was one of 2025’s best games and one of the best third-party releases ever to join Game Pass day-and-date. Players have now had over a year to finish the turn-based RPG, but for any subscribers who haven’t yet taken the plunge, time is running out. The GOTY winner is leaving Game Pass on October 15.

That leaves you just under two weeks to go and complete the journey or start it from scratch. You can rush the main story to clear it in under 30 hours, but if you want to mine all of the expanded content, a completionist run will take you more than twice that. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of the rare JRPG-inspired games that’s managed to break through in the modern era to a broader audience, in part thanks to its novel dodge and parry mechanics which inject some fresh energy into the usual turn-based grind. It’s also worth making it all the way through to hit the twist ending .

But Clair Obscur is also not the only great game leaving Game Pass this month . The full list includes:

Pacific Drive and A Plague Tale Requiem are both excellent, especially for the spooky month. The former is a sci-fi survival crafting game about navigating a zone full of strange anomalies with a haunted station wagon. The latter is about surviving a late medieval Europe infested with disease carrying rats. Donut County , on the other hand, is a light hearted puzzle game you can finish in just a few hours that is still one of my favorite indie games of all time.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 "broke" T-Pain with its "too sad" intro: "It gets worse? Absolutely not"
items.summary: Might I recommend The Last of Us?
items.content:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

(Image credit: Sandfall Interactive) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Some people just aren't built to endure the kind of bleak, unrelenting tragedy that often exists at the bottom of a great story's emotional arc. Rapper T-Pain may just have that affliction, having recently started Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on his Nappy Boy Gaming YouTube channel and noped out after its notoriously sad opening sequence.

*Spoilers for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 below. Turn back if you haven't played through the prologue yet.*

In the video just below, you can see T-Pain playing about 15 minutes of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 from the very start, which of course means he witnesses the awfully tragic death of Sophie in the prologue, leaving him speechless for a few seconds as he resumes control of Gustave. T-Pain eventually makes an exacerbated "shewwww" sound and exits to desktop. "Is it a sad story?" an offscreen person says, clearly noticing T-Pain's emotional exhaustion. "Yeah."

"Yeah, it was too sad," T-Pain responds, laughing. Just before ending the video, the rapper appears to read a comment on his stream warning him that, "it gets worse" – and anyone who's played through the game knows it absolutely does get worse, and soon – and T-Pain decides then and there, "Absolutely not."

I never want to play the best-written Blood of Dawnwalker mission ever again The 25 best video game stories of all time Troy Baker says The Last of Us 2's devastating final scene was originally at the start of the game This Game Broke T-Pain - YouTube Watch On I totally get his reluctance to continue here. Sometimes I just want to play a game, or watch a movie, or read a book, and not feel like I need to text my therapist. Unfortunately, in my view, if a story's writing and performances are effective enough to evoke such powerful emotion, it's probably worth seeing through, even if it never provides the sort of emotional upswing you want.

The Last of Us is one of my all-time favorite stories across all mediums precisely because it offers such an uncompromising, realistic account of two normal people trying to navigate a zombie apocalypse. Bad things are going to happen to good people, and there won't always be a picture-perfect redemption for anyone. Casting aside the conventional trajectories of heroes and villains makes for a much more believable, and thus absorbing story. You might not be moving your body like a cyclone afterwards, but you can always get low with something a little lighter to balance things out.

Elden Ring and Dark Souls inspired Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 director's approach to the RPG's story – "I didn't want to spoon-feed the player"

items.title: Clair Obscur Expedition 33 Director Comments on Sandfall's Next Game
items.summary: Sandfall Interactive doesn't seem too worried about living up to GOTY expectations
items.content:
By Polygon Staff & Willa Rowe Published Sep 14, 2026, 1:06 AM EDT FYI Sandfall Interactive doesn't seem too worried about living up to GOTY expectations

Image: Sandfall Interactive/Kepler Interactive Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google Discover Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , the debut game from developer Sandfall Interactive, was a smash hit in 2025 and earned numerous game of the year awards . The studio's next project, whatever it may be, might not be as popular. Director Guillaume Broche knows Clair Obscur is a tough act to follow, and he's OK if no one likes what the studio does next.

In a lengthy episode of Video Game Club on the Konbini YouTube channel in July, Broche discusses Sandfall's next game and says, "Maybe people won't like it. That's life." It is a surprisingly laid-back attitude toward following up one of the most beloved games in recent memory. For Broche, it isn't any different from the ethos he and the rest of the team at Sandall Interactive had while making Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . "We didn't make the first game to please anyone," he confesses, "and I think that's why it worked." Rather than pleasing an imaginary audience, Broche reveals that development on Clair Obscur was focused on satisfying the developers. They made a game that excited them. It was just an added bonus that plenty of players enjoyed the game as well.

The process obviously worked, and Broche sees no reason to mess with it, despite mounting expectations brought on by the success of Clair Obscur . He admits that there is definitely pressure to make things bigger or to expand the studio because of the attention Sandfall Interactive now has for its next project. Ultimately, Broche says that this would only result in the studio making games that he doesn't actually want to play.

As for Sandfall's next project, Broche declined to share details but did reveal the team will make some drastic decisions. A big question is whether the studio's next game will be a sequel to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . In the interview, Broche reiterates the idea he's shared before that "Clair Obscur" is the name of the franchise and Expedition 33 is just one story the team wanted to tell. This could mean Sandfall will take an anthology approach like in Final Fantasy , with each entry introducing a new world and cast of characters. Returning to the world of Expedition 33 in a true sequel would also require Sandfall to choose a canon ending for the game, something the studio has deliberately avoided. In any case, whatever follows Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 will be worth watching.

items.title: 5 Best Video Games Like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: If you enjoyed Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and are looking for more games that have a similar feel or play style, here are five that should tickle your fancy.
items.content:
Sandfall Interactive Add SVG on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover One of the best video games of 2025 was "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33," developed by French studio Sandfall Interactive. Among the best RPGs outside of "Final Fantasy," the game relies on turn-based combat as it weaves an engrossing epic tale with memorable characters. The story is set in a fantasy vision of France's Belle Époque as a group of adventurers set out to save their community from a mysterious villain known as the artist. With a dazzlingly original world brought to life by sharp writing and engaging gameplay, "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" reminds gamers what's possible with turn-based RPGs.

Of course, "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" has worn its influences on its sleeve and there are plenty of similar turn-based RPGs worth giving a try. From the games that inspired the 2025 title to releases that have gameplay systems that resemble "Clair Obscur," we've rounded up our favorites. Many of these games are cornerstones in the industry when it comes to stellar turn-based RPGs. These are the five best video games like "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" that fans should check out next.

Nintendo Nintendo and Square formed a tight partnership during the Super Nintendo era, with acclaimed titles like "Chrono Trigger" and "Secret of Mana" coming to the console. One game during this period that feels notably similar to "Clair Obscur" is "Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars," originally released in 1996. The game has Mario join a new team of friends, including Geno and Mallow, as they battle the villainous Smithy Gang that's invading the Mushroom Kingdom. Combat unfolds from a turn-based system, but real-time elements are included to make techniques more effective when input properly.

While "Super Mario RPG" is the most playful game on this list in regard to its tonal qualities, its gameplay mechanics definitely serve as a precursor for "Clair Obscur." But the game is a bold reinvention of what a "Super Mario" title can be, further proving that Nintendo's flagship character was more than a platforming protagonist. Nintendo released a remake of "Super Mario RPG," reimagining the classic for the Switch in 2023, wisely staying faithful to the SNES source material. While the Nintendo game and "Clair Obscur" may not share that much at first glance, that combat system and its surprisingly deep world connects the two titles.

Sony Interactive Entertainment Nearly 30 years after its initial release, "The Legend of Dragoon" is among the forgotten PS1 exclusives. A medieval fantasy RPG for a console with a game library full of them, the 1999 title follows the protagonist Dart searching for the figure who murdered his parents. Dart is joined by several playable allies in the campaign who gain the ability to temporarily transform into magical beings through what's referred to as a Dragoon Spirit. The game's combat system is its most unique aspect, revolving around turn-based inputs but in a quick time event sequence to string together combos.

It's this combat system and the general aesthetics around "The Legend of Dragoon" that reminds us of "Clair Obscur" when we play it. This is augmented by the game's transformation mechanic, allowing access to different and more powerful techniques for each character. Through a prominent use of its richly rendered in-game cinematics, the game also places a strong emphasis on its narrative, adding to the stakes. While overshadowed by titles like "Final Fantasy" and "Chrono Cross" on the PS1, "The Legend of Dragoon" definitely deserves more recognition.

Square Enix Of all the "Final Fantasy" games that align with "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33," the closest the fan-favorite franchise gets is "Final Fantasy X." A title from 2001 that changed gaming forever , the story has an athlete named Tidus who is transported to the world of Spira. Teaming up with a group of adventurers, including the powerful summoner Yuna, Tidus sets out to stop the villainous Sin from destroying the world. The game's combat system returns to more traditional turn-based gameplay rather than the Active Time Battle mechanics in prior entries, which included real-time elements.

Just looking at the broader narrative, "Final Fantasy X" and "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" both have a similar setup and stakes, albeit executed in very different ways. But the extensive party system in "Final Fantasy X" also evokes "Clair Obscur," allowing players to freely swap out members in combat. "Final Fantasy" has since largely moved away from turn-based combat, but "Final Fantasy X" still maintains its fun factor 25 years later. One of the best "Final Fantasy" games of all time , "Final Fantasy X" redefined the franchise for the 21st century.

Sega The "Persona" RPG series has been a staple for 30 years and feels bigger than ever, especially in regard to international audiences instead of only its native Japan. The best in the franchise to date is "Persona 5," originally released in 2016 for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation 4. Since then, the game received an enhanced remaster, rebranded as "Persona 5 Royal" in 2019 while significantly expanding its availability on other platforms. The game's story has its protagonist, Joker, transfer to a new high school and tap into his powers to take on shadowy supernatural threats.

"Persona 5" is an ambitious blend of RPG combat, dungeon-crawling exploration, and social simulator elements within the context of its high school setting. Somehow, all of these disparate elements come together beautifully, with its dungeon-crawling planning complementing its combat system especially well. Like "Clair Obscur," the game also has a striking menu layout that keeps players engaged with the action, never overstaying its welcome. Perfectly accessible if you've never played another game in the series, "Persona 5" is a modern RPG masterpiece.

Sega While the "Yakuza" series was initially built around real-time third-person beat'em-up gameplay, the franchise pivoted in a big way with "Yakuza: Like a Dragon." The 2020 game introduces new protagonist Ichiban Kasuga but also pivots to turn-based combat instead of the series' typical real-time brawling. The game also shifts its setting to Yokohama as Kasuga tries to make a name for himself in the world of organized crime in Japan. Kasuga can recruit parties of up to four characters to participate in these battles, mixing hard-hitting action with the series' penchant for wacky humor.

The shift to turn-based gameplay that "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" took could've turned out disastrously in lesser hands, but the game gives the whole series a fresh energy that elevates it as it solidifies its place in the current console generation. The game also incorporates quick time mechanics that help enhance the combat, keeping players engaged both defensively and offensively, like "Clair Obscur" and its own combat timing. "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" provides a boldly new direction for the long-running series.

items.title: Clair Obscur Expedition 33: Small Team, Massive Game Clip #1
'It's Incredibly Well-Made, But…' — Former PlayStation Boss Warned Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Devs It Would Be 'Overlooked' if They Called It a Turn-Based RPG
items.summary: Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it.
items.content:
Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it."

Yoshida, who served as PlayStation's head of indies and president of Sony Interactive Entertainment Worldwide Studios before stepping down in 2024, spoke about some key advice he gave the award-winning team during a recent lecture for indie game developers. Portions of that lecture were then reported by 4Gamer and subsequently translated by Automaton , including one piece of advice he gave to publisher Kepler Interactive while advising the team ahead of its April 2025 launch.

"It’s incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG," Yoshida warned the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 devs. "That alone might cause players to overlook it."

But why? Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 went on to receive praise from fans and critics (including a 9/10 review from IGN), while ending its already explosive year with big wins across The Game Awards , BAFTA , DICE , and IGN award shows. Its positive reception was so intense that even the developers at Sandfall Interactive weren't prepared for its towering Metacritic score .

Yoshida acknowledged Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 as a quality release long before it reached the hands of the public. He was impressed early on, calling attention to its "combination of turn-based JRPG mechanics and real-time action inputs reminiscent of The Legend of Dragoon." The problem, however, was that, at the time, he was concerned its success could be affected by what he observed to be a tendency for turn-based JRPGs to be seen as outdated.

Game-award-winning formula or not, Yoshida feared Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 would be ignored by some gamers if they saw that "turn-based" label. As a result, Kepler got creative and instead started selling Sandfall's first game as an experience with "reactive turn-based battles" instead, and the rest is history.

The game, of course, went on to become a massive sales success despite its proximity to the launch of The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion . Yoshida said he's since noticed an uptick in reports from publishers receiving pitches for new turn-based RPGs.

While we wait to see what's next from Yoshida and Sandfall, you can see why the developers behind Final Fantasy Resonance think turn-based RPGs are making a huge comeback . You can also read the devs' conversation about canon endings and the writer who got their start at Sandfall .

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 & the Beauty of a Non-Definitive Ending
items.summary: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 gives Maelle and Verso two painful endings. This feature examines grief, escapism, and why neither choice is wrong.
items.content:
Imagine: it’s PAX West 2025, and you’re me, wandering the expo hall with hundreds if not thousands of others. It’s a sea of people, but amongst them, you start to notice an incredibly peculiar pattern: dotting the crowd are bright red French berets. You cross direct paths with someone and notice their red beret is not only accompanied by a black-and-white striped shirt, but a red checked sash, strapping a fake plastic baguette to their back. You’re immediately both intrigued and perplexed, and raise the obvious question to your partner, who explains it’s from that game he started playing “with Charlie Cox in it”.

In this scenario, you are very much a fan of Charlie Cox and his starring in Daredevil, so you’re immediately reminded of what he’s talking about in that explanation – Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. You vaguely remember seeing the first casting announcement trailer for it during a random State of Play one early morning and getting excited because Daredevil(!), but ultimately you ended up going back to your endless, hellish cycle of Marvel Rivals lobbies when the game actually released. The red berets are a kind reminder of your previous excitement about the game, though, and it isn’t long after that you find yourself glued to your television while being serenaded by a beautiful French accent as you are formally introduced to the citizens of Lumiere. Your four years of French classes throughout school surely prepared you for this moment.

What you aren’t prepared for is just how much of an effect this game has on you by the end.

Now, at the risk of being honest, it’s a complete understatement to say I love this game. If you have interacted with me within the last year, I have talked to you about this game, or I have told you to finish it after you told me you didn’t even get through Act I, or I have endlessly gushed over Lorien Testard’s soundtrack what was probably an annoying amount. It’s rare to find yourself so committed to a piece of media, if only because you see yourself reflected in it so wholly, whether it’s in Maelle’s escapism or Verso’s self-sacrificial tendencies. After all, you don’t win 37 awards because people just feel pretty okay emotions about your game. As is with any piece of media, though, comes what others have to say about it.

(Obligatory note: What’s discussed going forward is riding off of the notion that the person reading this has played the game. If you haven’t, maybe go open Steam or the PlayStation store, grab some tissues, strap in for a bit, and hopefully you will thank me later. Or feel free to keep reading – I’m certainly not stopping you).

One of the gaming community’s most divisive conversations regarding Expedition 33 is regarding the two distinct endings the game has to offer, notwithstanding how both are unique in how they highlight the game’s central theme around the idea of grief. There hasn’t been a day that’s gone by in recent memory where I haven’t been faced with someone explaining how “[insert your preferred character’s name] ending is the right one”, or “if you chose [insert your not-preferred character’s name] ending, you’re clearly heartless”.

In the first ending, the audience is brought back to Lumiere after Maelle and Verso’s battle, and we see that Maelle has not erased the canvas, which was her motivation by the end of Act III. We’re rejoined by the ensemble we’ve grown to love, the Expeditioners as well as Esquie and Monoco, and we even see that Gustave and Sophie have both been repainted after their previous deaths. We’re also faced with Maelle and a considerably older Verso. We see Verso struggle for an uncomfortable moment, his hands stretching out and freezing over keys of a grand piano in Lumiere’s opera house, until it can be discerned Maelle uses her Paintress abilities in order to force the painted version of her late brother to play.

The colors are washed. The lighting is dimmed. It doesn’t yield much comfort aside from the embrace of familiar faces, but that just might be enough.

The second ending is an intentionally stark contrast. For the first time in the game, we’re officially brought outside of the canvas now that it’s presumably been destroyed, as that was Verso’s desire by the end game, and we’re shown the Dessendre’s. In front of them sits a grave donning the name “Verso Dessendre”. Renoir and Aline share a tender embrace in front of their son’s grave, Clea leaves behind a bouquet of achingly familiar red and white flowers before excusing herself, and we see a scarred Alicia– or Maelle– standing by as she watches the scene unfold, holding a sewn Esquie doll. The camera turns and we see the images of the very same Expeditioners, including Gustave and Verso’s painted self, framed by the Eiffel Tower as they wave goodbye before dissipating.

The colors are bright. It’s backlit by a sunny day. The comfort is uncertain and bittersweet, but it’s ultimately not an unwelcome feeling, either.

Undeniably, the discussion around these endings is, of course, typically viewed as black-and-white as possible. More often than not, when faced with multiple endings by the end of a game, audiences are used to getting a “good” ending and a “bad” ending, leaving little room for discussion. And, in these cases, that is the game’s intent. In these cases, the games do have a black-and-white, a good-and-bad. It’s not unheard of for a game to punish a player for making poor choices throughout a play through. When looking at Expedition 33’s endings, though, this mindset is frankly doing a disservice to the game’s theming as a whole.

Grief as a theme is interwoven throughout the entire game, and when is the process of grieving ever black-and-white? Grief by all accounts is an incredibly non-linear process. We have all grieved over someone, over something, and we all understand what that means. Both of the endings evoke very different emotions, but it really is up to the player and what they choose to prioritize within their own grief. Yes, in Maelle’s ending, we see the way she chooses to use her Paintress abilities against her brother and father’s wishes, but more importantly, she’s also surrounded by those she has come to love, in a fully-functioning body. She’s given grace to those who have only ever lived inside of the canvas, reasserting the idea that they are sentient individuals with their own lives and autonomy, despite the circumstances they were painted into. Within Verso’s ending, the Dessendre’s are now able to work on moving past their shared grief regarding the loss of their real-life brother and son after years of stagnation, but at the cost of Alicia having a healthy physical body, and at the loss of everyone we have come to love inside of the canvas.

Both of these endings offer a resolution and catharsis in their own ways, and the outcome of one doesn’t make the other more or less right. When discussing these endings, we can’t assume why someone chose one ending over the other, because their grief surrounding the game is ultimately their own, and it’s not up to us to dictate how that feels to them. It can’t be stressed enough how sacrificing nuance in these discussions doesn’t only do a disservice to the game, but also the players and their own emotions about it.

I have a confession to make: I wholeheartedly chose Maelle’s ending the first time I played, and at that moment, it wasn’t a difficult choice for me. It made sense. I had grown so incredibly fond of Lumiere and the canvas and those inside of it, just like Maelle, but I saw myself in so many facets of her. I was a sixteen-year-old girl once, finding escape in worlds I created and in the media I was in love with, be it novels or games or movies, in order to remove myself from the very real grief I was experiencing. It’s something I still find myself doing even in adulthood, and ironically, probably the reason why I found myself so absorbed in Expedition 33 in the first place. The hours I put into the game were the direct result of me needing a distraction from life, and to watch the game slowly begin to unveil what it truly was felt like looking into a mirror. Of course I chose to save Lumiere. Of course I sided with Maelle. It’s what I do all the time. More often than not, I run from my grief rather than let myself feel it, and instead I look for reassurance and acceptance and comfort in worlds where my real feelings can’t hurt me. It’s far easier to feel for the characters on my screen than it is to feel for myself. After all, their emotions aren’t tangible, unlike my own. Expedition 33 was the first time I had ever personally experienced a piece of media that conveyed that feeling in a way that felt so specific, and so undeniably real.

items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of the rare games that reminds me why I fell in love with video games in the first place, and it's a great experience on Steam Deck after some tweaks.
items.content:
Action RPG, Adventure, JRPG, Open World, Souls-Like

Every once in a while, you come across a piece of media that resonates with you for years on end. The emotional impact, countless hours spent absorbing the music, characters, atmosphere; it all comes together to create something uniquely mesmerizing. The kind of experience that makes you silently realize you’re deep into one of your favorite games of all time.

Clair Obscur is the very first game from indie studio Sandfall Interactive, and before release, almost nobody expected it to become such a massive hit and dominate award shows the way it has. This small team of 33 passionate French developers delivered something gigantic, and its impact will likely leave a mark on the overall gaming industry for years to come.

Set in a breathtaking dark fantasy world inspired by the Belle Époque golden age in France, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 tells the story of a civilization slowly approaching extinction. Every year, a mysterious being known as the Paintress awakens and paints a number upon a massive monolith. Anyone matching that age instantly vanishes without a trace. With the number decreasing year after year, humanity sends an expedition into the unknown each time, hoping to find the Paintress and finally end the cycle. Expedition 33 follows the 67th expedition, a group of people marching toward an almost impossible mission, knowing that their own remaining time is running out. What follows is an emotional and deeply personal journey filled with loss, mystery, and the constant fear of inevitable death.

The story and writing are etched with a level of screenplay and dialogue quality that competes with film classics. Without diving into spoilers, the narrative constantly evolves through multiple emotional and philosophical layers. Much of the experience revolves around mystery, slowly connecting fragmented conversations, hidden meanings, and puzzling dialogue pieces together. That constant feeling of trying to understand the truth behind everything is what made the story so addictive.

Clair Obscur distinguishes itself from its peers through its characters. From major cast members to side characters you may only speak to once, nearly everyone feels carefully written and memorable. One of the smartest decisions in the script is that no character feels completely devious or maligned. The game masterfully captures the grey areas of humanity, constantly pushing the player to empathize with actions that may be wrong, desperate, or forced by circumstances.

Story and writing are personally the most important aspects of a video game for me. With most games, I usually find myself nitpicking certain flaws or decisions I didn’t fully like. But in Expedition 33’s case, I genuinely struggle to think of anything I would change. The writing quality throughout the experience is nothing short of masterful. It made me cry, laugh, reflect, and constantly kept me emotionally invested from beginning to end. It was a complete rollercoaster of emotions.

When it comes to gameplay, my favorite way of describing Expedition 33 is “the best of both worlds.” The combat system feels like a near-perfect blend of classic turn-based Final Fantasy combat and the reaction-based defensive mechanics of Souls-like games such as Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice . While adding active reaction mechanics into turn-based games is not an entirely new concept, Expedition 33 is in a class of its own.

At first glance, combat starts like a traditional turn-based RPG. You build a party with different characters, unique strengths, playstyles, and skill combinations, carefully strategizing your way through encounters. However, once enemies begin attacking, the game transforms into something far more interactive. You can dodge, parry, or jump over attacks entirely through player reaction and timing.

Parrying, in particular, becomes one of the most satisfying mechanics in the game. It is extremely difficult to master, but also incredibly rewarding. Every successful parry grants AP, allowing you to build resources even while defending. Perfectly parrying entire enemy combos triggers devastating counterattacks that feel impactful every time. After hundreds of hours of gameplay, landing a full counter never stops being satisfying.

There are a total of six playable characters in the game, and each of them feels both unique and surprisingly deep mechanically. Each character introduces their own gameplay system and combat identity. For example, Lune functions as a mage who utilizes elemental “Stains” to create different effects and empower specific abilities, while Sciel fights using a card-based system that grants buffs, applies debuffs, and shifts her between different combat stances and modes.

items.title: 1st Anniversary of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33

Expeditioners!! 

 

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy! 

8 Million Copies Sold

We're so thrilled, and honestly still quite overwhelmed, to announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has officially reached 8 million copies sold!

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

Game Update: New Haircuts + Patch Notes

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Community Emotes

Our community is packed with phenomenally talented artists and we wanted to celebrate that today.  

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

Official Baguette Merch

In the mood to add some baguette to your wardrobe? 

We’ve partnered with Orcival and Le Béret Français to bring you the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 striped shirt and beret for your cosplays! 🥖    You can purchase the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Orcival mariniere here

And the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Le Béret Français beret is available to buy here

On top of that, keep an eye out for a limited number of units of the Monolith Set to be back in stock from our partners at Laced and Pix n' Love soon!! 

And Finally… Cake

It's been a big day for us. Thank you for making it possible. 🎂 

And if you know someone who wants to pick up the game, we're running a 20% sale right now on Steam - As well as some fun merchandise goodies available on our merch page!

Merch Page

From the bottom of our hearts, we’re so thankful to each and every one of you – this has been the best year of our lives, thanks to you. 

 

- The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is '95 percent' made with Blueprints
items.summary: Sticking to a nearly-vanilla version of Unreal Engine kept Sandfall Interactive on track.
items.content:
Keep up with the latest news, interviews, talk coverage, and other game dev insights from GDC right here on Game Developer. Read More

Sticking to a nearly-vanilla version of Unreal Engine kept Sandfall Interactive on track.

Much has been made of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developer Sandfall Interactive's production process. As you've probably heard by now, the smash hit game was produced by a studio that employs fewer than 40 people, and everyone in the game industry has a hot take about what made that possible (and often ignore the hundreds of other people listed in the game's credits ).

They've been so prolific that at a GDC Festival of Gaming talk from Sandfall chief technical officer Tom Guillermin and senior gameplay programmer Florian Torres had an entire slide advising the audience not to use their presentation as a roadmap. "This is not meant to be a tutorial or like a how-to guide on how to make games," said Guillermin. "It's a retrospective on how we made Expedition 33 ."

But let's face it, when your studio's first game is such a highly-polished hit, everyone will obviously be trying to copy your homework. Developers aiming to learn about Sandfal's process swarmed Moscone West, and let out a collective murmur of shock when Guillermin and Torres described how their small team of programmers supported such an expensive-looking game—they just used a near-vanilla version of Unreal Engine.

Related: Clair Obscur writer shares production advice that could improve your game's story

And they didn't use Unreal Engine to write lines and lines and lines of code in C++. Expedition 33 was largely made with Unreal's Blueprints system.

According to Torres, 95 percent of the game was constructed in Blueprints.

For the uninitiated, Unreal Engine's Blueprints system is a visual scripting tool that lets developers link "nodes" together to create different gameplay elements. It's used to define object-oriented objects or classes in the game engine. For laypeople, this mean it lets developers assemble game logic by stringing together nodes of scripting logic without constantly coding in C++.

On Clair Obscur , this meant that Guillermin, Torres, and the rest of the programmers could hand off content and feature development to the studio's designers and artists, allowing them to produce and test content in the game engine with fewer roadblocks that would rely on a programmer to create code.

Unreal Engine developers use Blueprints to different degrees. The system is deeply tied into Unreal Engine's natural codebase, and if you need to modify the engine in any way, the system becomes less reliable. In fact Guillermin said that Sandfall has a very "vanilla-first" approach when it comes to using Unreal. "We take all the tools that are natively present and we push them to their to their limits so we don't have to develop bespoke tools for the features and content of the of the game," he said.

Related: Moonlighter developer delays public playtest of next game over concerns of AI cloning

Photo via the author, slide by Sandfall Interactive

The only "modifications" they used were old-fashioned Unreal plugins like CommonUI, GeometryScripting, ALS (Advanced Locomotion System) and KawaiiPhysics (which one commentator on Bluesky described as "one guy's freeware project for doing swooshy anime hair physics.")
